$comment: What agentlings may reach outside their sandbox. A connection declares its
own default with 'defaultOn'; the user's departures from those defaults are
recorded in .agentlings/settings.json, never here. Secrets are named, never
written here — put the value in .env under that name, or paste it in
Settings, which validates it with one real call and writes the same file
(D-078). 'setup' holds the plain-words steps that drawer shows. A
connection whose secrets are missing is never live, whatever its default
says.
'web' is built in and defaultOn: this is an outreach platform, so reaching
a page is what the crew is for rather than something to be asked for job by
job. Switch it off in Settings. It is our own fetch, which returns readable
text trimmed to maxChars rather than a whole page. Add hosts to 'allow' to
narrow it.
Every connection lists the 'tools' a job may call on it. The list is the
grant: a server offering both reading and acting can be adopted for
reading alone by naming only its reading tools, and anything not named is
refused by the allowlist. It also makes this file say what a connection
can do without anyone having to run it.
'browser' is Playwright MCP (Apache-2.0, Microsoft), fetched by npx so no
code lands in this repo. It is deliberately READ-ONLY: of the 24 tools it
offers, the eight named below read a page and none of them act. Left out
on purpose are click, type, fill_form, press_key, select_option, drag,
drop, file_upload, handle_dialog, evaluate, run_code_unsafe and
network_request — because this app's safety model is a sandbox reviewed
before anything is promoted, and a submitted form cannot be reviewed
afterwards. Adding an acting tool is a decision about that model, not a
line in a list.
It signs in by re-using a session you created yourself: log in once in a
real browser, save the storage state, and point AGENTLINGS_BROWSER_STATE
at the file. The app never sees a password — and with the variable unset
the argument is dropped and browsing works signed out.
'github' is builtin rather than an MCP server, and that is a decision
(D-040). The reference GitHub MCP server is deprecated by npm, and the
supported replacement ships as Docker or a remote HTTP endpoint that this
registry cannot express. Builtin is the better answer regardless, for the
reason given below about stdio budgets: a code host is exactly where an
unbounded reply hurts, since one issue list or one diff can be enormous.
Owning the call means owning the size of the answer, so every tool returns
compact lines and none of them returns a patch. It reads and cannot act:
of the 26 tools the reference server exposes, the 12 that create, update,
comment, merge, push or fork are absent, and catalog.test.ts asserts it.
It needs GITHUB_TOKEN in .env and is never live without one.
'search' is builtin for the same reason as 'github', and exists because of
a measured failure (D-053): the crew could read a page you named and never
find one, and a missing capability is substituted rather than refused — one
run answered from model knowledge and said so, another spent its whole
budget driving the browser at a search engine and died. A search API answers
in verbose JSON, so owning the call owns the size: what comes back is three
fields a result, enough to choose a URL and hand it to fetch_page. The two
tools compose and both trim. It needs BRAVE_API_KEY in .env and is never
live without one; it ships off, like everything credentialed.
Brave rather than Google, and that is not a preference — Google Custom
Search stopped being a general web search on 20 January 2026. Engines
created after that date can only search up to 50 domains you nominate, and
existing whole-web engines lose it on 1 January 2027. It was built against
Google first and reverted when the console refused to enable the toggle
(D-054). Scraping the search page is not the fallback: it is against the
terms, and D-035 measured what it returns to a crawler anyway — 429 and a
CAPTCHA, which is the wall the run in D-053 died against.
External MCP servers take: name, label, description, transport 'stdio',
command, args, tools, and optional secrets {ENV_NAME: 'why it is needed'}.
They ship off by default — they carry credentials and act on the user's
behalf, which is a different decision from reading a page. Keep results
small by design — every token a tool returns is a token the model pays to
read, and for a stdio server that budget is the server's own flags, not
ours: the SDK talks to it directly, so nothing of ours sits in between.
'telegram' is the first sending connection, and it grants a session
NOTHING: its tools list is empty on purpose, and catalog.test.ts asserts
it stays that way. A run asks to send by writing OUTBOX.json in its
sandbox; review shows the messages; approving replays them through the
bot with the token from .env — the session never holds the token and has
no tool to send with (D-075). The switch still gates it like any
credentialed connection: off, or missing its secret, means Approve
refuses with the reason. 'to' in an outbox message is a numeric chat id —
a bot can only message people who tapped Start on it once, which makes
the reachable audience exactly the people who opted in.
'google' is the second sender and the first OAuth connection (D-080). It
grants a session nothing, exactly like telegram — the gmail channel sends
an approved outbox as the user, from their own address. Its secrets are
the user's OWN OAuth client (never a shared one: restricted Gmail scopes
on a shared client mean Google verification and a paid audit, D-076) plus
the refresh token the Connect flow stores after consent happens on
Google's own page. One consent covers gmail.send, calendar.events and
contacts.readonly, so later capabilities need no re-consent. The consent
screen must be PUBLISHED to production — left in Testing, Google expires
the refresh token every 7 days and sends refuse with a reconnect message.
'whatsapp-business' is the third sender (D-081), same shape: empty tool
grant, sends only at approval. Business-initiated WhatsApp is
pre-approved templates — Meta owns the template's text, so an outbox
carries the template name + language once and per-recipient params, and
review shows all of it. Two secrets, validated together with one real
call, because the call needs both. Per-message pricing is Meta's, by
category and country; the optional WHATSAPP_USD_PER_MESSAGE in .env is
the user's own declared rate and is stamped on sends.jsonl as such —
never a guess. Start with the free test number Meta gives every app: it
messages up to 5 numbers you verify, which is the whole demo loop.
'render' is builtin and defaultOn like 'web', and reaches nothing: it
prints a run's own HTML into a styled PDF through the Edge this machine
already has (playwright-core by channel — no browser download, D-128).
The render is offline — every request the page makes is aborted — so the
document must be self-contained: inline CSS, data: images, @page rules
for size and margins. The reply is bytes the runner writes at the
sandbox root; base64 never rides a prompt.
render_plate (D-143) is the same door pointed at level backdrops: the
page renders at 2000×900, is screenshotted once it sets document.title
to 'ready', and comes back quantized to the 128-colour backdrop budget
with crew separation measured — the receipt carries the same numbers the
pack checker holds a plate to. One stated exception to the offline rule:
http://three.local/three.module.js (and the core file it imports) is
fulfilled from the server's own pinned copy of three.js and never leaves
the machine; every other URL still aborts.
'calendar' is the first READING sibling on the Google consent (D-158). It
declares the same three GOOGLE_OAUTH_* secrets the Connect flow stores, so
it is ready the moment 'google' is and never before — but it carries its
own switch and its own tools list, because one switch must never gate both
reading and sending, and 'google' stays a sender that grants a session
nothing. The one tool reads events off the user's primary calendar as
compact lines, times as the calendar states them. There is deliberately no
compiled-tool door for it: a desk brief is live-data judgement work, so a
method that read the calendar must never compile into a $0 tool that runs
with nobody looking (D-158's uncompilable-by-construction).

connections.name: web
connections.label: Read web pages
connections.description: Fetches a page and returns its readable text, trimmed. No JavaScript, no sign-ins.

connections.name: render
connections.label: Print HTML to PDF, render backdrop plates
connections.description: Renders a run's own self-contained HTML through the system Edge, offline — into a styled PDF, or a 2000×900 level-backdrop plate quantized to the backdrop budget. External URLs are blocked during the render; three.js is served from the server's own pinned copy.

connections.name: github
connections.label: Read a code host
connections.description: Reads issues, pull requests, commits and files from GitHub. A run reads and cannot act — the one write is a comment you approved at review, replayed by the server like every send (D-104).

secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN: a GitHub token with read access to the repositories the crew should see — add Issues write access if you want approved comments to post

setup: Open github.com → Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained personal access tokens
Generate a token with read-only access to the repositories the crew should see
Paste it here — it is sent to api.github.com only

connections.name: search
connections.label: Search the web
connections.description: Finds pages by searching, and returns titles, snippets and links. Reading one is a separate step — hand a link to the web connection.

secrets.BRAVE_API_KEY: a Brave Search API key — free tier at brave.com/search/api

setup: Create a free key at brave.com/search/api
Paste it here — it is sent to api.search.brave.com only

connections.name: bls
connections.label: US labour statistics
connections.description: Reads US Bureau of Labor Statistics series — consumer prices, unemployment, payrolls — by series id, newest observations first. A registered key gets 500 calls a day and up to 50 series in one call; without one the only route is the keyless allowance, a shared bucket that is usually already empty.

secrets.BLS_REGISTRATION_KEY: a BLS API registration key — free at data.bls.gov/registrationEngine

setup: Register free at data.bls.gov/registrationEngine — the key arrives by email
Paste it here — it is sent to api.bls.gov only, in the request body

connections.name: calendar
connections.label: Read your calendar
connections.description: Reads the events on your own Google Calendar — times, titles, what still awaits your reply, who is invited, where. Rides the same Google sign-in as sending, behind its own switch; reading grants no way to change anything.

secrets.GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID: the google connection's OAuth client id — stored by its Connect flow, nothing new to paste
secrets.GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: that client's secret — stored by the same Connect flow
secrets.GOOGLE_OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN: the refresh token the Connect flow stores after you approve on Google's page

setup: Nothing to paste here — press Connect on the 'Send Gmail, as you' connection; one consent already covers reading the calendar
Then switch this on: it only gates reading, and sending stays the google connection's own switch

connections.name: browser
connections.label: Use a web browser
connections.description: Opens pages in a real browser and reads what they show, including sites that need JavaScript. Reads only — it cannot click, type or submit anything.

connections.name: telegram
connections.label: Send Telegram messages
connections.description: Sends messages through your Telegram bot when you approve a reviewed outbox. Grants the crew no tools at all — sends happen at review, never inside a run.

secrets.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN: a bot token from @BotFather — the bot can only message people who tapped Start on it

setup: Open Telegram and message @BotFather
Send /newbot and pick a name — it answers with a token
Paste the token here
Anyone the crew should message taps Start on your bot once

connections.name: google
connections.label: Send Gmail, as you
connections.description: Connects your Google account by OAuth. Sends approved outbox mail from your own address, and creates approved calendar events on your own calendar — both on the one consent. The crew gets no tools from it.

secrets.GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID: your own OAuth client's id — created once in Google Cloud, steps in Settings
secrets.GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: that client's secret — Google treats a desktop-app secret as non-confidential
secrets.GOOGLE_OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN: stored by the Connect flow after you approve on Google's own page

setup: Create a project at console.cloud.google.com (free) and enable the Gmail API
OAuth consent screen: External, add yourself, then PUBLISH to production — an app left in Testing logs you out every 7 days
Credentials → Create credentials → OAuth client ID → application type: Desktop app
Paste the client id and secret here and press Connect — your password is typed on Google's page, never here

connections.name: whatsapp-business
connections.label: Send WhatsApp Business messages
connections.description: Sends pre-approved template messages through Meta's Cloud API when you approve an outbox. Arrives from your business number, priced per message by Meta. The crew gets no tools from it.

secrets.WHATSAPP_TOKEN: a permanent System User access token from Meta Business with whatsapp_business_messaging permission
secrets.WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID: the sender number's id from the app's WhatsApp settings — an id, not the phone number itself

setup: Create an app of type Business at developers.facebook.com and add the WhatsApp product
Start with the free test number Meta gives the app — it can message up to 5 numbers you verify
Business settings → System users → generate a permanent token with whatsapp_business_messaging
Copy the Phone number ID from the app's WhatsApp → API Setup page
Create a message template and wait for Meta to approve it — business-initiated sends are templates only
Paste the token and the phone number id here, then Check — one real call proves both

connections.name: slack
connections.label: Send Slack messages
connections.description: Posts messages as your own Slack bot when you approve a reviewed outbox. The crew gets no tools from it — sends happen at review, never inside a run.

secrets.SLACK_BOT_TOKEN: the Bot User OAuth Token (xoxb-…) from your own Slack app — it can only post where the bot has been invited

setup: Create a Slack app at api.slack.com/apps — From scratch, pick your workspace
Under OAuth & Permissions, add the bot scope chat:write (add chat:write.public to post in public channels without an invite)
Install the app to the workspace — it answers with a Bot User OAuth Token (xoxb-…)
Paste the token here, then Check — one real call says which bot and workspace it is
For private channels, /invite the bot in Slack first
